html:
The Din-i Ilahi, "religion of God", was a small circle of disciples that the Mughal emperor Akbar formed around himself in 1582. It grew out of years of debate between faiths at his court.

In 1575 Akbar built a hall called the Ibadat Khana, the house of worship, at Fatehpur Sikri. On Thursday nights he first heard Sunni scholars argue. Disgusted by their quarrels, he opened the hall to Shias, Hindus, Jains, Parsis and, from 1580, Jesuit priests from Goa. In 1579 a decree made him the final judge when Muslim scholars disagreed.

He came to hold that every religion had some truth and none had all of it. His rule of government was sulh-i kul, peace with all. He had already ended the tax on non-Muslims in 1564, and he married Rajput princesses who kept their own worship.

The Din-i Ilahi had no scripture, priests or temples. Members honoured the sun and fire as signs of God, gave up meat on some days and vowed loyalty to the emperor. Fewer than twenty joined, and only one of them, Birbal, was a Hindu. The court historian Abul Fazl praised it; the orthodox Badauni called it a turn away from Islam. It ended with Akbar's death in 1605.
sum: The Din-i Ilahi, "religion of God", was a small circle of disciples that the Mughal emperor Akbar formed around himself in 1582. It grew out of years of debate between faiths at his court.
